draft.title: Controlling blood glucose
card: Cells use glucose for energy, so blood glucose must stay within a narrow range. The pancreas detects changes in blood glucose and releases hormones in response.
a hormone released when blood glucose is high, such as after a meal. It helps cells take up glucose, and the liver and muscles store it as glycogen. Blood glucose falls.
a hormone released when blood glucose is low, such as between meals. It causes the liver to break down glycogen into glucose and release it into the blood. Blood glucose rises.
Each hormone reverses the change that triggered it. This is negative feedback, so blood glucose returns to its normal range.
draft.remember: High glucose brings insulin, which lowers it. Low glucose brings glucagon, which raises it.

a.q: Which response happens after a person eats a large meal and their blood glucose rises?
opts: The pancreas releases more insulin
The pancreas releases more glucagon
The liver breaks down glycogen to glucose
The pancreas stops detecting blood glucose
a.why: High blood glucose triggers insulin, which helps cells take up glucose and lets it be stored as glycogen. Glucagon is tempting, but it raises blood glucose, so it would push the level further from normal.

b.q: Priya has not eaten for several hours and her blood glucose has fallen below its normal range. What happens next?
opts: Glucagon is released and the liver releases glucose
Insulin is released and cells take up more glucose
Glucagon is released and the liver stores more glycogen
Insulin is released and the liver breaks down glycogen
b.why: Low blood glucose triggers glucagon, which makes the liver break down glycogen and release glucose into the blood. Glucagon is paired with storing glycogen in the second wrong option, but storing glucose would lower blood glucose further.
b.clue: The response must reverse the fall, so glucose has to enter the blood.

b.best: Glucagon is released and the liver releases glucose

problems.detail: Why (b) refers to 'the second wrong option', but options are shown in random order, so students may not see that option second. Name the option by its content instead, for example 'the option pairing glucagon with storing glycogen'.

check.summary: The card and both questions are accurate, and each question has one clear answer. The only problem is that Why (b) refers to 'the second wrong option', which won't match the randomised option order.
